subject: System Design — Building Blocks
summary: High-level design (HLD) interviews test whether you can turn a vague prompt — "design Instagram" — into a justified architecture in 45 minutes, and every justification leans on the same dozen building blocks: load balancers, caches, CDNs, replicas, shards, queues, and the consistency trades that connect them. Companies test this because the blocks are the shared vocabulary of production engineering; a candidate who can compute that a workload is 500:1 read-heavy and conclude "cache-first, CDN for media" is demonstrating judgment, not memorisation. This subject teaches each block the same way: the problem it exists to solve, the mechanism with concrete numbers, the failure mode interviewers probe (stampedes, split brain, resharding pain, duplicate deliveries), and the exact moment in an interview to reach for it. Study it by doing, not reading: for every section, redraw the ASCII diagram from memory, re-derive the worked estimates on paper, and rehearse the "reach for this when..." line out loud — the interview is a spoken performance, and the flashcards at the end are calibrated to the numbers and one-liners you must be able to say without pausing.

sections.title: 1. How an HLD Round Works: the 5-Step Script
sections.content:
Start with what the round is actually testing, because most first-timers get this wrong. A high-level design (HLD) interview is not a quiz on Kafka settings. The interviewer hands you a vague sentence — "design Instagram" — and watches whether you can turn it into a scoped, justified architecture, out loud, inside 45 minutes. Candidates fail by drawing boxes in minute two, before anyone agreed on what the system must do. The fix is a script. Use the same five steps every time, with a time budget, and say the step names out loud so the interviewer can follow your plan.

```
 0-5 min   REQUIREMENTS   functional (what the system does) +
                          non-functional (scale, latency,
                          availability vs consistency)
 5-10 min  ESTIMATES      QPS, storage, bandwidth — order of
                          magnitude only
10-15 min  API            3-5 endpoints with request/response
15-30 min  HIGH-LEVEL     boxes + arrows, walk one request
                          through the whole picture
30-45 min  DEEP DIVE      1-2 components, chosen together
                          WITH the interviewer
```

Requirements: ask three to five questions, then write the answers down where both of you can see them. Functional requirements are features ("post a photo, follow a user, see a feed"). Non-functional requirements are numbers and guarantees ("100M daily active users, feed loads under 200 ms, we prefer availability over consistency for the feed"). Explicitly park what you will NOT build ("no DMs, no Stories") — scoping out is a skill they grade.

Estimates: five minutes of arithmetic (next section) that decides whether you even need sharding or a CDN. The numbers must drive the design; an estimate you never use again is theater, and interviewers notice.

API: three to five endpoints, e.g. POST /photos, GET /feed?cursor=..., POST /follows. Nail down the ID format and pagination here, because the deep dive will depend on both.

High-level: client -> DNS -> load balancer -> app servers -> cache -> database, plus a queue and a CDN where the estimates earned them. Walk one read and one write through the diagram end to end before adding anything fancy.

Deep dive: ask "would you like me to go deeper on feed generation or on the storage layer?" Steering the conversation is itself being tested — a senior engineer checks alignment before spending twenty minutes on the wrong thing.

In the interview, reach for this script whenever the prompt is open-ended. When the interviewer interrupts with a new constraint ("what if it's 10x the traffic?"), they are testing adaptability: update the estimate and revise the diagram, do not defend the old one.

sections.title: 2. Back-of-Envelope Estimation: the Numbers You Memorise
sections.content:
Why this exists: every architecture decision is a claim about numbers. "We need a cache" means "the database cannot serve this read QPS at this latency." If you cannot produce the numbers, every choice you make is a guess, and interviewers probe exactly there. You need three things memorised: a latency table, one QPS shortcut, and byte sizes.

The latency table (rounded, modern hardware — the ratios matter more than the digits):

```
L1 cache reference ............   0.5 ns
Main memory reference .........   100 ns
Compress 1 KB (fast codec) ....     2 us
SSD random read (4 KB) ........   100 us
Round trip inside datacenter ..   500 us
Read 1 MB sequentially, SSD ...     1 ms
HDD seek ......................    10 ms
Read 1 MB sequentially, HDD ...    20 ms
Same-continent network RTT ....    50 ms
Cross-continent network RTT ...   150 ms
```

Read it as ratios: memory is ~1000x faster than an SSD random read, which is ~1000x faster than a cross-continent round trip. That single line explains caching (move data from SSD to memory) and CDNs (move data across the world toward the user).

QPS math. A day has 86,400 seconds; round it to 10^5 for mental math. So X million requests per day is about 10X requests per second: 100M requests/day ~ 1,000 QPS average. Peak traffic is 2-5x average (say which you assume). Storage math: one character is one byte, an ID or timestamp is 8 bytes, and the ladder is KB -> MB -> GB -> TB -> PB, a thousand each step.

Worked estimate 1 — photo sharing, 100M DAU:

```
writes: 100M DAU x 0.1 uploads/day = 10M/day ~ 100 w/s, peak ~500
reads:  100M DAU x 50 views/day = 5B/day    ~ 50,000 r/s
read:write = 500:1  --> cache + CDN earn their place
media:  10M x 2 MB = 20 TB/day  (~7 PB/year --> object store + CDN,
        this will never live in a relational database)
metadata: 10M x 200 B = 2 GB/day --> a sharded DB holds years of this
```

Worked estimate 2 — URL shortener, 100M new links/month:

```
writes: 100M / (30 x 86,400 s) ~ 40 w/s        (tiny)
reads:  100:1 ratio --> ~4,000 r/s, peak ~20,000
storage, 5 years: 100M x 12 x 5 = 6B rows x 500 B ~ 3 TB
key space: base62, 62^7 ~ 3.5 x 10^12 --> 7 characters is enough
```

Notice what the numbers say: the shortener's data fits on one machine — you shard (split data across machines) for availability and read QPS, not for size. The photo app is the opposite: storage volume, not QPS, is the first monster.

In the interview, reach for estimation right after requirements, and then USE the results: say "500:1 read-heavy, so the design is cache-first" out loud. When the interviewer asks "how much storage in year one?", they are testing whether your architecture came from arithmetic or from a memorised YouTube diagram.
sections.code:
SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86_400
GB = 10**9
TB = 10**12

def avg_qps(requests_per_day):
    return requests_per_day / SECONDS_PER_DAY

# URL shortener: 100M new links/month, 100:1 read ratio, 500 B/row
writes_per_day = 100_000_000 / 30
w_qps = avg_qps(writes_per_day)
assert 35 < w_qps < 45, w_qps            # ~39 writes/sec
r_qps = w_qps * 100
assert 3_500 < r_qps < 4_500             # ~3,900 reads/sec
rows_5y = 100_000_000 * 12 * 5
total = rows_5y * 500
assert 2.9 < total / TB < 3.1            # ~3 TB in 5 years

# Photo app: 100M DAU
uploads = 100_000_000 * 0.1
media_per_day = uploads * 2_000_000      # 2 MB per photo
assert abs(media_per_day / TB - 20) < 1  # ~20 TB/day of media
meta_per_day = uploads * 200
assert abs(meta_per_day / GB - 2) < 0.2  # ~2 GB/day of metadata

print(f"shortener: {w_qps:.0f} w/s, {r_qps:.0f} r/s, {total/TB:.1f} TB/5y")
print(f"photo app: {media_per_day/TB:.0f} TB/day media, {meta_per_day/GB:.0f} GB/day metadata")

sections.title: 3. Load Balancing: L4 vs L7, Algorithms, Health Checks
sections.content:
The problem first: one application server has a ceiling — a few thousand requests per second, one power supply, one process that can crash. The moment your QPS estimate exceeds one machine, or the moment you promise availability, you need several servers plus something that spreads traffic across them and hides the dead ones. That something is a load balancer (LB).

```
              +----------------+
  clients --> | load balancer  | --> server A   (healthy)
              |  (L4 or L7)    | --> server B   (healthy)
              +----------------+ -X> server C   (failed health
                                     check - removed from pool)
```

L4 vs L7 is the classic follow-up. An L4 load balancer works at the transport layer (it sees IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports, never the content), so it forwards packets with very little work — extremely fast, millions of connections, but it cannot tell /api from /images. An L7 load balancer works at the application layer: it terminates TLS (decrypts the connection) and reads the HTTP request, so it can route by path (/api to the API pool, /static to the asset pool), by header, or by cookie, and it can do sticky sessions (pinning one user to one server). The price is more CPU per request. Practical rule: L7 (nginx, Envoy, an AWS ALB) in front of web applications; L4 (an AWS NLB) when you need raw TCP throughput or non-HTTP protocols — database traffic, game servers, gRPC at extreme scale.

Algorithms, with the reason each exists. Round robin (take turns) is the default and assumes servers and requests are equal. Weighted round robin fixes unequal servers (the new box with 2x CPU gets 2x traffic). Least connections fixes unequal requests: when some requests run 10x longer than others, take-turns piles work on unlucky servers, so route each new request to the server with the fewest open connections. Hash-based (by client IP or a key) gives stickiness, useful when servers keep local state — and consistent hashing (section 6) is the robust version of this.

Health checks are what turn a traffic-spreader into an availability tool. Active checks: the LB calls GET /health on every server every few seconds and ejects a server after, say, 3 consecutive failures, re-admitting it after it passes again. Passive checks: the LB watches real traffic and ejects servers that return errors or time out. Without health checks, the LB keeps sending every Nth user into a dead machine — your availability story collapses.

In the interview, reach for a load balancer the moment you draw a second server — and name the layer. When the interviewer asks "L4 or L7 here?", they are testing whether you know that path-based routing, TLS termination, and sticky sessions are L7 features, and that L4 buys throughput by staying blind to content. Also mention that the LB itself must not be a single point of failure: two LBs with a shared virtual IP, or DNS in front.

sections.title: 4. Caching: Patterns, Eviction, and the Stampede
sections.content:
Why caches exist: your estimate said reads outnumber writes 500:1, and the latency table said memory (100 ns) beats an SSD database read (100 us) by ~1000x. Most real workloads are also skewed — a small fraction of keys gets most of the traffic — so keeping the hot set in memory removes the bulk of database load. The standard tool is Redis: an in-memory key-value store doing sub-millisecond reads at roughly 100K ops/sec per node. It sits between your app servers and the database, and doubles as the home for sessions, rate-limit counters, and leaderboards.

Cache-aside (lazy loading) is the default pattern — the application owns the logic:

```
        1. GET user:42
app ------------------> cache
        2. MISS
app <------------------ cache
        3. SELECT ... WHERE id=42
app ------------------> database
        4. row
app <------------------ database
        5. SET user:42  (TTL 300s + random jitter)
app ------------------> cache
```

Only requested data gets cached, and if the cache dies the app still works (slower — every request falls through to the DB, which is why "what if Redis goes down" is really a question about whether your DB survives the full read load). Costs: the first read of any key is slow, and between a DB write and the next cache refresh, readers see stale data. On writes, the usual move is to update the DB then DELETE the cache key (invalidation), letting the next read repopulate.

Write-through flips ownership: every write goes to cache and database synchronously, so reads rarely miss — at the price of slower writes and caching data nobody may read. Write-behind (write-back) acknowledges the write after updating only the cache and flushes to the DB asynchronously: very fast writes, but if the cache node dies before the flush, those writes are gone — acceptable for view counters, unacceptable for orders.

Eviction: memory is finite, so the cache discards entries. LRU (least recently used — evict what has gone longest without access) is the default because hot data is usually recently used. LFU (least frequently used) resists one-off scans better. TTL (time-to-live) is an expiry stamp per key and is your staleness bound.

The cache stampede — also called the thundering herd — is the favourite follow-up. A hot key (the homepage feed) expires; in the next 50 ms, 10,000 concurrent requests all miss and all fire the same expensive query at the database, which falls over; the outage cascades. Three fixes, in the order to say them: (1) per-key single-flight — the first miss takes a lock (SET key_lock NX in Redis) and rebuilds while everyone else waits or briefly serves the old value; (2) stale-while-revalidate — keep serving the expired value while one background refresh runs; (3) TTL jitter — add a random offset to every TTL so a deploy-time batch of keys does not expire in the same second.

In the interview, reach for cache-aside plus Redis by default, and volunteer the stampede fix before being asked — when the interviewer asks "what happens when a hot key expires?", they are testing whether you have seen (or foreseen) a real production incident, not whether you can define TTL.
sections.code:
from collections import OrderedDict

class LRUCache:
    """The default eviction policy, in 15 lines: an ordered dict where
    'recently used' means 'moved to the end'."""
    def __init__(self, capacity):
        self.cap = capacity
        self.d = OrderedDict()

    def get(self, k):
        if k not in self.d:
            return None                    # cache MISS
        self.d.move_to_end(k)              # mark as most recently used
        return self.d[k]

    def put(self, k, v):
        if k in self.d:
            self.d.move_to_end(k)
        self.d[k] = v
        if len(self.d) > self.cap:
            self.d.popitem(last=False)     # evict least recently used

c = LRUCache(2)
c.put("a", 1); c.put("b", 2)
assert c.get("a") == 1                     # touch "a" -> "b" becomes LRU
c.put("c", 3)                              # over capacity -> evicts "b"
assert c.get("b") is None
assert c.get("a") == 1 and c.get("c") == 3
print("LRU ok: evicted the least recently used key, kept the touched one")

sections.title: 5. CDN: Beating the Speed of Light
sections.content:
The problem a CDN solves is physics, not code. Light in fiber takes ~150 ms for a cross-continent round trip, and no amount of server tuning changes that. If your origin servers (the machines you actually run) live in Virginia and your user is in Delhi, every image, script, and video segment pays that tax — and a web page makes dozens of such fetches. Meanwhile the content is identical for everyone. Serving identical bytes from far away is pure waste.

A CDN (content delivery network) is a globally distributed cache: hundreds of edge locations, also called PoPs (points of presence), each near users. DNS steers each user to the nearest edge. The edge serves cached content at ~10-30 ms instead of ~150-200 ms and, as a bonus, absorbs traffic that never reaches your origin — often 90%+ of total bytes.

```
user (Delhi) --20ms--> edge PoP (Mumbai) --HIT--> respond, done
                            |
                            | MISS (first request per object)
                            v
                     origin (Virginia)   ~200 ms away
                     edge stores the object, TTL from
                     the Cache-Control header
```

Two operating modes. A pull CDN fetches from the origin on the first miss and caches by TTL — no upload workflow, the default for websites. A push CDN is one you upload content to ahead of time — used when you control publishing moments, like a video platform pre-positioning a new episode before release. What belongs on a CDN: images, video segments, JS/CSS bundles, fonts, mobile app downloads — and, at bigger scale, even cacheable GET API responses (edge caching), which is worth mentioning as a bonus point.

Invalidation is where interviews go next: what happens when you ship app.js v2 but edges hold v1 for another 24 hours? The clean answer is versioned URLs — put a content hash in the filename (app.8f3ab2.js) and reference the new name from your HTML. Old and new versions coexist; nothing needs purging; caches can hold assets "forever" (a TTL of a year). Purge APIs exist but are slow to propagate and easy to forget; hashed filenames make the problem structurally disappear.

One trap worth naming: a CDN helps static and cacheable content. Your personalised feed, your cart, your account page still travel to the origin, which is why global apps eventually run origins in multiple regions — a different, much harder problem (multi-region replication).

In the interview, reach for a CDN the moment the product contains media or a global audience — say "2 MB photos times 50K reads/sec is 100 GB/s; that bandwidth must terminate at edges, not at my origin." When the interviewer asks "how do users get the new version of a cached file?", they are testing whether you know cache invalidation by version rather than by hope.

sections.title: 6. Databases at Scale: Replicas, Sharding, Consistent Hashing
sections.content:
A single database node handles a few thousand QPS and a few TB comfortably; beyond that you scale in a fixed order, because each step buys the most with the least pain. Step one: add read replicas — copies of the database that receive every write from the primary and serve reads. Since most workloads are read-heavy (your 500:1 estimate), replicas multiply read capacity cheaply. The cost is replication lag: a replica may be seconds behind, so a user can write and then read the old value (section 10 fixes this). Step two: cache in front (section 4). Step three — only when writes or data size outgrow one machine — shard.

Sharding (also called partitioning) splits data across machines by a shard key. Three strategies. Range sharding: users A-F on shard 1, G-M on shard 2 — range scans stay cheap, but popular ranges become hot shards (all of today's data on the "newest" shard). Hash sharding: shard = hash(user_id) % N — spread is even, but range queries now touch every shard. Directory-based: a lookup service maps key -> shard — maximum flexibility (you can move one big customer to a dedicated shard), at the cost of an extra hop and a new critical dependency. Choosing the shard key is the real decision: it must spread load evenly AND match your access pattern, because any query that lacks the shard key must fan out to all shards, and cross-shard joins and transactions become application-level work.

Now the resharding pain, which is where interviewers steer. With hash(key) % N, adding a single node changes N to N+1 and remaps almost every key — with 4 nodes replacing 3, about 75% of keys move at once: a massive data migration plus a cold cache everywhere, triggered by the routine act of adding capacity.

Consistent hashing fixes this. Picture the hash space 0..2^32 bent into a ring. Both nodes and keys are hashed onto the ring; each key belongs to the first node clockwise from it.

```
                 0
           .-----------.
          /             \
     N3  *               *  N1
         |   hash ring   |
         |               |
          \             /
           *-----.-----*
          N2      \
                   * key K --clockwise--> owner is N2

  add N4 between N3 and N1:
    only keys in the arc (N3 -> N4] move, ~1/N of all keys
    everything else keeps its owner - caches stay warm
```

Adding or removing a node now moves only the keys in one arc — about 1/N of the total — instead of nearly all of them. One refinement to mention: with few nodes, arcs are uneven, so each physical node is placed on the ring many times as virtual nodes (100+ points per server), which evens out the load and lets a node's departure be absorbed by many peers instead of one. This is how Cassandra and DynamoDB place data and how load balancers do sticky routing that survives pool changes.

In the interview, reach for replicas and caching first and say so — sharding is the last resort because it complicates every query forever. When the interviewer asks "what happens when you add a shard?", they are testing whether you know mod-N breaks and can explain the ring. Name your shard key and defend it against the hot-partition question ("celebrity user" is the classic).

sections.title: 7. Replication and Leader Election: Sync, Async, Split Brain
sections.content:
Why replicate at all: disks die, machines reboot, datacenters lose power. If the only copy of an order row lives on one disk, your durability equals that disk's lifespan. Replication keeps N copies on independent machines, which buys durability (data survives a dead disk), availability (a live copy keeps serving), and read scale (section 6). The standard shape is leader-based: one leader accepts all writes and streams them to followers.

The first fork in the road is sync vs async replication, and it is a straight trade of latency against data loss. Synchronous: the leader waits for a follower to confirm before acknowledging the client — if the leader dies one millisecond later, the write exists elsewhere; zero loss on failover, but every write pays a network round trip, and a slow follower slows all writes. Asynchronous: the leader acknowledges immediately and ships the write in the background — fast, but on a crash the last few seconds of acknowledged writes may exist nowhere else and are lost when a follower is promoted. Middle path worth naming: semi-synchronous — wait for exactly one follower (or a quorum), tolerating the rest lagging. Banking ledgers take sync; like-counts take async; most systems take the middle.

Now failover. The leader dies; the followers must agree which of them becomes the new leader — that agreement is leader election, and it is done with a consensus protocol (Raft, Paxos) or delegated to a coordination service that implements one (ZooKeeper, etcd). The core rule is quorum: any decision needs a majority, floor(N/2)+1 nodes. Five nodes need three; a cluster of five tolerates two failures.

The reason majority is sacred is split brain: a network partition (nodes alive but unable to reach each other) can leave two groups each believing the other is dead. If both sides elect a leader, both accept writes, and the datasets diverge — reconciling two histories of the same account balance has no good answer. Quorum prevents it structurally: two disjoint majorities cannot exist, so at most one side can elect.

```
              network partition!
   +------------+     X X X     +------------------+
   |  A    B    |               |  C    D    E     |
   |  2 nodes   |               |  3 = MAJORITY    |
   +------------+               +------------------+
   cannot elect                 elects new leader,
   (2 < 3, no quorum)           term/epoch += 1
   old leader here must
   STOP accepting writes
```

One more safeguard to name: fencing tokens. Elections are numbered (a term or epoch); every write carries the current term, and storage rejects writes stamped with an old term. So a deposed leader that never noticed the election — frozen in a long GC pause, then waking up — has its writes refused instead of corrupting data.

In the interview, reach for this whenever you have drawn a "primary DB", because "what happens when it dies?" is guaranteed. The strong answer names the chain: heartbeat timeout detects death, a quorum elects, clients re-route (via the LB or a config service), and you state the data-loss window explicitly — "async replication, so we can lose up to ~1 s of acknowledged writes; for payments I would use semi-sync." That last sentence is what separates a memorised diagram from an engineer.

sections.title: 8. Message Queues: Async Work, Delivery Guarantees, Kafka vs RabbitMQ
sections.content:
Start with the failure that motivates queues. Checkout calls the email service synchronously; the email provider has a bad minute; now checkout times out and you lose orders because a receipt was slow. Synchronous call chains couple your availability to your weakest dependency and your latency to your slowest one. A message queue breaks the coupling: the producer (checkout) appends "send receipt for order 831" to the queue and returns immediately; the consumer (email worker) processes at its own pace; if it is down for an hour, messages wait. The queue also absorbs spikes — a flash sale writes 50K orders/min into the queue while workers drain at their steady 10K/min — and lets producer and consumer teams scale and deploy independently.

Delivery guarantees are where interviewers separate readers from practitioners. At-least-once is the honest default: the queue redelivers any message not acknowledged (consumer crashed after doing the work but before acking) — so duplicates are a fact of life, and every consumer must be idempotent (safe to run twice; see section 11). At-most-once (ack before processing) risks silent loss and is rarely acceptable. "Exactly-once delivery" across independent systems is not achievable in general — the ack itself can be lost — so the phrase to say is effectively-once: at-least-once delivery PLUS idempotent processing, via a dedupe table keyed by message ID, or a transactional outbox (write the DB row and the outgoing message in one DB transaction, then a relay publishes it). Kafka's "exactly-once semantics" is real but scoped to Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines; the moment you touch an external system, you are back to idempotency.

The two mental models:

```
KAFKA - a distributed, partitioned, append-only LOG
producers        topic "orders"
  P1 --\   +--------------------------------------+
  P2 ----+>| partition 0: [m0][m1][m2][m3]  ----> |--> consumer C1 (offset 2)
  P3 --/   | partition 1: [m0][m1][m2]  --------> |--> consumer C2 (offset 3)
           +--------------------------------------+
  messages are KEPT (days); consumers track offsets;
  replay = rewind the offset; order holds per partition;
  a consumer group splits partitions among its members

RABBITMQ - a smart BROKER that routes and forgets
  producer -> exchange --(routing rules)--> queue -> worker
  message is deleted after ack; rich routing (topic,
  fanout, priorities, per-message TTL); a task dispatcher
```

Choose by shape of the problem. Kafka when data is a stream of events that several independent consumers read at their own pace (analytics + search indexer + fraud detection all reading "orders"), when you need replay after a bug, or when throughput is huge (millions of msgs/sec, since appending to a log is nearly free). RabbitMQ when the unit is a job to be done once by one worker — send this email, resize this image — with routing rules, priorities, and simple operations. Rough scale: Kafka throughput is 10-100x RabbitMQ's; RabbitMQ latency and per-job ergonomics are better for classic task queues.

In the interview, reach for a queue whenever a step does not need to happen before you respond to the user — emails, thumbnails, feed fan-out, analytics — or when write spikes exceed what the database absorbs. When the interviewer asks "what if a message is processed twice?", they are testing whether you know at-least-once is the reality and idempotency is the answer, not whether you can recite "exactly-once".

sections.title: 9. CAP and PACELC in Practice
sections.content:
CAP is misquoted so often that stating it correctly is itself a signal. The theorem: when a network partition happens (P — nodes are alive but cannot reach each other), a distributed system must choose between consistency (C — every read sees the latest write, or fails) and availability (A — every request gets an answer, possibly stale). The key corrections to the folklore version: this is not "pick any two of three." Partitions are not optional — cables get cut, switches die, GC pauses look like partitions — so P is a fact, and the real choice is C-or-A during a partition only. On a healthy network you can have both. And a "CA distributed system" is not a thing; a single-node database is CA because it cannot partition with itself.

What the choice looks like concretely. CP (consistency over availability): during a partition, the minority side refuses writes and possibly reads — users see errors, but nobody ever sees wrong data. Pick CP for money movement, inventory decrement at checkout, seat booking, and coordination itself (ZooKeeper/etcd are CP — a lock service that hands the same lock to both sides of a partition is worse than one that is down). AP (availability over consistency): both sides keep answering with what they have and reconcile later — pick AP for like counts, view counters, product-page reads, shopping-cart contents (Dynamo's famous example: losing a cart addition costs more than showing a briefly stale cart). Cassandra and Dynamo-style stores default AP.

PACELC extends CAP to the part of life CAP ignores: the 99.9% of time with no partition. If Partition, trade A vs C; Else, trade Latency vs Consistency. The "else" is the everyday cost: strong consistency requires coordination (sync replication, quorum reads), and coordination is round trips, and round trips are latency. Dynamo-style systems are PA/EL — available under partition, fast in normal operation, eventually consistent. HBase/BigTable-style systems are PC/EC — consistent always, paying latency for it.

```
              is the network partitioned?
              /                        \
            YES                         NO (normal day)
           /    \                     /              \
     choose C    choose A        low LATENCY      strong CONSISTENCY
     refuse or   answer with     async repl.,     sync repl., quorum
     error       possibly        local reads      reads, extra RTTs
                 stale data
        CP          AP               EL                  EC
```

The senior move is refusing to label a whole system. One application holds both: payments are CP, the feed is AP; the order row is EC, the recommendation widget is EL. Per-feature classification is exactly what "design Instagram" wants when consistency comes up.

In the interview, reach for CAP vocabulary when the interviewer asks "what happens during a network partition?" or "is this strongly consistent?" — they are testing whether you can map a business operation to a concrete failure behaviour ("during a partition, checkout on the minority side returns an error and retries; the feed keeps serving stale data"). Saying "we sacrifice consistency" without naming what the user experiences is the junior version of the answer.

sections.title: 10. Consistency Models: Strong, Eventual, Read-Your-Writes
sections.content:
The problem: the instant you have replicas, "the value" of a key stops being one thing — there are several copies, briefly disagreeing. A consistency model is the promise you make to readers about which copy they may see. Interviews care about three levels and one worked failure.

Strong consistency (linearizability): the system behaves as if there were a single copy — once any client's write is acknowledged, every subsequent read anywhere sees it (or something newer). This is what a single-node database gives you for free and what distributed systems pay for with coordination: writes wait on replicas or reads consult a quorum, adding round trips (the EL/EC trade from PACELC). Eventual consistency is the other end: replicas receive updates asynchronously, and the only promise is that if writes stop, all replicas converge. A read meanwhile may return stale data. That sounds academic until you watch it break a user experience:

```
 t0  user uploads new avatar --> LEADER   (write acked)
 t1  change is in flight to the replica (async, lag ~2 s)
 t2  user refreshes their profile
     load balancer sends the read --> REPLICA
     replica still has the OLD avatar --> "my upload failed?!"
     user uploads again, files a bug, or leaves
 t3  replica applies the change - too late, trust is gone
```

The user does not need global strong consistency; they need read-your-writes consistency — the guarantee that a user always sees their OWN writes, while everyone else can lag. Between strong and eventual live several such session guarantees, and naming them precisely is a strong signal. Implementations of read-your-writes, in the order to offer them: (1) after a user writes, route that user's reads to the leader for a window longer than typical replication lag (pin by user ID for ~5 s); (2) sticky sessions — a user talks to the same replica, which has seen their writes; (3) version tokens — the write returns a log position (LSN); the client sends it with reads, and a replica serves the read only once it has replayed past that position.

Two siblings worth one sentence each. Monotonic reads: a user never sees time run backwards (refresh shows a comment, next refresh loses it — caused by bouncing between replicas with different lag; fix with sticky routing). Causal consistency: effects never appear before causes — a reply must never be visible before the message it answers, even if they came from different users to different replicas.

In the interview, reach for this vocabulary whenever the interviewer asks "is eventual consistency acceptable here?" — the test is whether you can map a guarantee to a user-visible harm. The strong answer pattern: "For the feed, eventual is fine — a follower seeing my post 3 seconds late harms nobody. For the author's own profile, I need read-your-writes, implemented by pinning the author's reads to the leader briefly. For balance transfers, strong consistency, paid for with quorum reads." Three features, three models, each justified.

sections.title: 11. Rate Limiting and Idempotency at the Edge
sections.content:
Two protections live at the front door of every serious API, and interviewers love them because both look small and both hide sharp edges.

Rate limiting first — the why: without it, one buggy client in a retry loop, one scraper, or one attacker consumes capacity you provisioned for everyone; overload then cascades (slow DB -> timeouts -> client retries -> more load). A rate limiter enforces a ceiling per key (user ID, API key, or IP) at the API gateway, before requests reach application servers. Rejected requests get HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header, which tells well-behaved clients when to come back.

Algorithms, each defined by the flaw of the previous. Fixed window ("100 requests per minute, counter resets at :00") is easy but bursty at the boundary: 100 requests at 11:59:59 plus 100 at 12:00:01 is 200 in two seconds while both windows say "fine". Sliding window fixes the boundary by counting the trailing 60 seconds (a log of timestamps, or the cheaper weighted sum of two adjacent windows). Token bucket is the practical favourite: a bucket holds up to `capacity` tokens, refilled at `rate` per second; each request spends one; an empty bucket means 429. It allows honest bursts (capacity) while enforcing a long-run average (rate) — two knobs that map directly to product language. Leaky bucket is its cousin that forces a perfectly smooth outflow. State lives in Redis (INCR + EXPIRE, or a small Lua script so check-and-decrement is atomic across gateway instances).

Idempotency — the why: retries are everywhere (client timeouts, at-least-once queues from section 8, users double-clicking "Pay"), so the same logical request WILL arrive twice. An idempotent operation is one where running it twice has the same effect as once. Reads and PUTs are naturally idempotent; "charge the card 500" is catastrophically not. The fix is the idempotency key: the client generates a unique key per logical operation (a UUID minted when the checkout page loads) and sends it in a header; the server atomically records the key with the stored response on first execution; a duplicate arrives, the server finds the key, and replays the stored response without executing again. Keys get a TTL (say 24 h). This is how Stripe's payment API works, which makes it a name worth dropping.

```
             +---------------------------+
 client ---> |  API GATEWAY              | ---> app servers
 key:        |  1. rate limit check      |
 user:42     |     token bucket in Redis |
 Idem-Key:   |  2. idempotency lookup    |
 uuid-9f3    |     seen key? -> replay   |
             |     stored response       |
             +---------------------------+
   over limit  --> 429 + Retry-After: 30
   duplicate   --> same 200 as before, card charged ONCE
```

In the interview, reach for both the moment the design touches money, orders, or any public API — and volunteer them before being asked: "POST /orders takes an idempotency key, so queue redelivery and client retries cannot double-charge." When the interviewer asks "which rate-limiting algorithm?", they are testing whether you know the fixed-window boundary burst and can explain token bucket's two knobs; when they ask "what if the same request arrives twice?", they are testing whether you connect retries, at-least-once delivery, and idempotency into one story.
sections.code:
class TokenBucket:
    """capacity = max burst; rate = sustained requests/sec."""
    def __init__(self, capacity, refill_per_sec):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.rate = refill_per_sec
        self.tokens = capacity
        self.last = 0.0

    def allow(self, now):
        elapsed = now - self.last
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + elapsed * self.rate)
        self.last = now
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False

tb = TokenBucket(capacity=3, refill_per_sec=1.0)

# burst at t=0: exactly `capacity` requests pass, the rest get 429
burst = [tb.allow(0.0) for _ in range(5)]
assert burst == [True, True, True, False, False]

# after 2 seconds, 2 tokens have refilled
assert tb.allow(2.0) is True
assert tb.allow(2.0) is True
assert tb.allow(2.0) is False              # bucket empty again

# idempotency: dedupe store replays the stored response
processed = {}
def charge(idem_key, amount, ledger):
    if idem_key in processed:              # duplicate -> replay
        return processed[idem_key]
    ledger.append(amount)                  # the real side effect
    processed[idem_key] = {"status": "charged", "amount": amount}
    return processed[idem_key]

ledger = []
r1 = charge("uuid-9f3", 500, ledger)
r2 = charge("uuid-9f3", 500, ledger)       # retry of the same operation
assert r1 == r2 and ledger == [500]        # charged exactly once
print("token bucket + idempotency key: burst capped, no double charge")

sections.title: 12. Observability: Why p99, Not Average
sections.content:
The problem: a distributed system fails in pieces — one replica lagging, one pod leaking memory, one dependency slow for 1% of calls — and without instrumentation you learn about it from angry users. Observability is the discipline of making the system explain itself, and it stands on three pillars. Metrics: numbers over time (QPS, error rate, latency percentiles), cheap to store, what you alert on. Logs: structured event records, expensive but detailed, what you search during an incident. Traces: the path of ONE request across services, stitched by a trace ID that every hop propagates — the only tool that answers "WHERE did this slow request spend its time?"

```
 trace 7f3a: GET /checkout                    total 480 ms
 |- gateway ....................   5 ms
 |- orders service ............   90 ms
 |    |- inventory service ....   40 ms
 |    |- orders DB query ......   30 ms
 |- payment service ...........  380 ms   <-- the culprit
```

Now the percentile lesson, which is the interview's favourite. Latency is not a bell curve — it is skewed with a long tail (GC pauses, cache misses, lock contention, that one replica). Averages hide the tail. Worked example: 100 requests; 99 finish in 50 ms, one takes 5 s. Average = (99x50 + 5000)/100 = 99.5 ms — a number describing not one single real request. The percentiles tell the truth: p50 (median) = 50 ms, p99 = 5 s. A p99 of 5 s means one user in a hundred waits five seconds — say it that way, as users, and dashboards start meaning something.

Why the tail matters more than 1% suggests: fan-out multiplies it. A page that calls 100 backends in parallel is as slow as its slowest call, and the chance that at least one of the 100 hits its own p99 is 1 - 0.99^100 ~ 63%. So "the worst 1%" becomes the median experience of your richest pages — this is Google's "tail at scale" argument, and quoting the 63% number is a strong senior signal. It is also why heavy users hurt most: they make the most requests, so they hit the tail most often.

The working vocabulary to deploy. SLI (service level indicator): the measured thing — "fraction of requests under 200 ms". SLO (service level objective): the target — "99.9% of requests under 200 ms over 30 days". Error budget: 100% minus the SLO — the amount of allowed failure; when the budget is spent, you stop shipping features and fix reliability. The four golden signals to monitor on every service: latency (p50/p95/p99, never the mean), traffic (QPS), errors (rate of 5xx), saturation (how full the constraining resource is — CPU, connections, queue depth). Alert on symptoms users feel (SLO burn), not on causes (CPU at 80%), or the on-call drowns in noise.

In the interview, reach for observability as the closing move of any design: "I would dashboard the four golden signals per service, alert on SLO burn rate, and propagate a trace ID from the gateway down." When the interviewer asks "how do you know your p99 regressed after a deploy?", they are testing whether you think of monitoring as part of the design or as somebody else's job.

interviewQA.q: Walk me through how you would spend the first ten minutes of a system design interview.
interviewQA.a: Minutes 0-5: requirements. I ask what the system must do (functional: post photos, follow, view feed) and pin the non-functional numbers that drive everything: how many daily active users, expected read/write ratio, latency targets, and whether we prefer availability or consistency for the core flows. I also state out-of-scope items explicitly, because scoping is graded. Minutes 5-10: estimation. I convert the agreed numbers into QPS and storage: 100M DAU at 50 feed reads/day is 5B reads/day, about 50K QPS average against maybe 500 writes/sec — a 500:1 read-heavy system, so the design will be cache-first with a CDN for media. I say the conclusion out loud so the interviewer sees the numbers driving the architecture, then sketch 3-5 API endpoints before drawing any boxes. The point of the ritual is that every later component gets justified by a number or a requirement, not by habit.
followUps: What do you do if the interviewer refuses to give you numbers and says 'you choose'?
How do you handle an interviewer who interrupts your script and asks you to jump straight to the deep dive?

interviewQA.q: Estimate the QPS and five-year storage for a URL shortener with 100M new links per month.
interviewQA.a: Writes: 100M per month over roughly 2.6M seconds is about 40 creates/sec — tiny. Redirects are read-heavy; assuming 100:1, reads are about 4,000/sec average, and I plan for a 5x peak, so 20K reads/sec. Storage: 100M x 12 months x 5 years = 6B rows; at ~500 bytes each (short code, long URL, owner, timestamps) that is about 3 TB. The interesting conclusion is that 3 TB fits on a single large machine — so if I shard, it is for read QPS and availability, not for capacity, and honestly a cache handles the read load first: redirects are immutable, so a Redis layer in front absorbs the hot keys and the hit rate will be very high. I would also check the key space: base62 with 7 characters gives 62^7 ~ 3.5 trillion codes, comfortably more than the 6B needed. The habit being tested is rounding aggressively (a day is 10^5 seconds) and then letting the numbers veto components I do not need.
followUps: The interviewer doubles the scale to 200M links/month — what actually changes in your design?
How would you generate the short codes without collisions across multiple app servers?

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between an L4 and an L7 load balancer, and when do you pick each?
interviewQA.a: An L4 load balancer operates at the transport layer: it sees IPs and TCP/UDP ports and forwards packets without reading content, which makes it extremely fast and able to hold millions of connections — but it cannot tell /api from /static. An L7 load balancer operates at the application layer: it terminates TLS and parses the HTTP request, so it can route by path, host, header, or cookie, do sticky sessions, retry failed requests, and serve as the natural home for rate limiting — at the cost of more CPU per request. My defaults: L7 (nginx, Envoy, ALB) in front of web and API traffic, because path routing and TLS termination are almost always wanted; L4 (NLB) for non-HTTP protocols and raw throughput — database connections, game servers, or as a fast front tier passing to L7 proxies behind it. I would also mention that the LB needs health checks to eject dead backends, and that the LB itself must be redundant — a pair sharing a virtual IP — or I have moved my single point of failure rather than removed it.
followUps: How does the load balancer decide a server is unhealthy, and what is the risk of an aggressive health check?
Your L7 LB terminates TLS — what are the security and performance implications of that choice?

interviewQA.q: Explain cache-aside. What are its failure modes?
interviewQA.a: Cache-aside means the application owns the caching logic: on a read it checks the cache first; on a miss it reads the database, then writes the value into the cache with a TTL; on a data change it updates the database and deletes the cache key, so the next read repopulates. Its virtues: only actually-requested data occupies memory, and the system survives a cache outage because every request can fall through to the database. The failure modes are the interview material. First, staleness: between a DB write and the delete (or if the delete fails), readers see old data — the TTL is the bound on how old. Second, the cold-start and stampede problem: a hot key expiring means thousands of concurrent misses hammering the DB with the same query; I need single-flight locking or stale-while-revalidate. Third, the 'cache down' scenario: if Redis dies, the full read QPS lands on the database, so I must check the DB survives that — otherwise the cache is load-bearing and needs replication of its own. Fourth, a subtle race: read-miss reads an old DB value, a write updates DB and deletes the key, then the slow reader populates the cache with the old value — mitigated by short TTLs or versioned writes.
followUps: When would you choose write-through or write-behind over cache-aside?
Why delete the cache key on write instead of updating it in place?

interviewQA.q: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
interviewQA.a: A stampede — the thundering herd — happens when a popular cached value expires and, in the tens of milliseconds before someone repopulates it, thousands of concurrent requests all miss and all send the same expensive query to the database. The database saturates, latency spikes, timeouts trigger retries, and the retries make it worse; caches that quietly carried 95% of your load reveal it all at once. Three fixes, and strong candidates name all three. One: per-key single-flight — the first request to miss acquires a short lock (SET stampede:key NX EX in Redis) and rebuilds the value; concurrent missers either wait briefly or serve the stale copy. Two: stale-while-revalidate — keep the expired value and serve it while exactly one background refresh runs, trading a few seconds of staleness for total protection of the DB. Three: TTL jitter — add a random offset to every TTL so keys cached together (after a deploy or cache flush) do not expire together. In an interview I volunteer this at the moment I draw the cache, because 'what happens when the hot key expires?' is nearly guaranteed as a follow-up, and the pattern applies beyond caches — connection retries and service restarts herd the same way.
followUps: Your whole Redis cluster restarts and the cache is empty — how do you bring the system back without killing the database?
How does exponential backoff with jitter relate to the same herd problem?

interviewQA.q: Why does hash(key) % N break when scaling, and how does consistent hashing fix it?
interviewQA.a: With mod-N placement, the shard for a key is a function of the total node count, so changing N changes almost every answer: going from 3 nodes to 4 remaps about 75% of keys. That means a huge simultaneous data migration, and every cache built on those keys goes cold at once — the routine act of adding capacity becomes a self-inflicted outage. Consistent hashing removes N from the formula. Hash both nodes and keys onto a ring of the hash space (0 to 2^32); a key is owned by the first node clockwise from its position. Adding a node claims only the arc between it and its predecessor, so about 1/N of keys move and everything else keeps its owner — caches stay warm, migration is proportional to one node's share. The refinement to mention is virtual nodes: with only a few physical nodes the arcs are lopsided, so each server is hashed onto the ring at 100+ points; load evens out, and when a node leaves, its keys scatter across many peers instead of dumping onto one neighbour. This is the placement scheme inside Dynamo-style databases and Cassandra, and load balancers use it for sticky routing that survives pool changes.
followUps: A celebrity key makes one arc of the ring hot — virtual nodes do not fix that. What does?
How does a Dynamo-style store use the ring to choose the N replicas of a key, not only the primary?

interviewQA.q: How do you shard a relational database, and how do you choose the shard key?
interviewQA.a: I shard only after read replicas and caching are exhausted, because sharding taxes every future query. The mechanics: pick a shard key, pick a strategy — range (contiguous key ranges per shard: range scans stay local, but hot ranges like 'this month' overload one shard), hash (even spread, but range queries fan out), or directory-based (a lookup service maps key to shard: flexible, one more hop and one more critical system). The shard key decision dominates: it must distribute load evenly AND appear in your dominant queries, because any query without it fans out to every shard, and cross-shard joins and transactions stop being SQL's problem and become my application's problem. For a multi-tenant SaaS I shard by tenant/user ID so a customer's data is colocated and most queries stay single-shard; the risk is the whale tenant, which is why the directory option ('move that tenant to a dedicated shard') stays attractive. I also plan resharding on day one — consistent hashing or a shard map I can edit — because hash-mod-N means remapping nearly everything when I grow. The interviewer is testing whether I know sharding's costs, not whether I can say the word.
followUps: A query needs data from all shards — say, 'top 100 posts today'. How do you serve it?
Instagram-style problem: one celebrity user's data overloads their shard. What are your options?

interviewQA.q: Synchronous versus asynchronous replication — what is the trade and when do you pick each?
interviewQA.a: It is a direct trade of write latency against data loss on failover. Synchronous: the leader waits for at least one follower to confirm the write before acknowledging the client, so an acknowledged write exists in two places — a leader crash loses nothing, but every write pays an extra network round trip and a slow or dead follower stalls all writes. Asynchronous: the leader acknowledges immediately and streams changes in the background — writes are fast and follower trouble is invisible, but when the leader dies, the last seconds of acknowledged writes may exist nowhere else; promote a follower and they are gone. The practical middle is semi-synchronous: wait for exactly one follower (or a quorum) and let the rest lag, bounding loss without paying for the slowest replica. Choice follows the cost of losing an acknowledged write: a payment ledger or inventory decrement takes sync/semi-sync and eats the latency; like counts, analytics events, and feed fan-out take async. In an interview I state the loss window in numbers: 'async with ~1 s lag means a failover can silently drop up to a second of acknowledged writes — acceptable for the feed, unacceptable for orders, so orders go semi-sync.'
followUps: With semi-sync to one follower, what happens if that particular follower becomes slow?
How does replication lag from async replicas leak into what users see, and how do you hide it?

interviewQA.q: What is split brain, and how do real systems prevent it?
interviewQA.a: Split brain is when a network partition divides a cluster into groups that cannot reach each other, and more than one group concludes it should lead — so two leaders accept writes for the same data simultaneously and the histories diverge. Merging two versions of the same account balance afterwards has no clean answer, which is why the cure is structural, not reactive. Prevention one: quorum. Any leader election requires a majority — floor(N/2)+1 — and two disjoint majorities cannot exist, so at most one partition side can elect; the minority side refuses writes and waits. This is also why clusters have odd sizes: five nodes tolerate two failures, and six nodes still tolerate only two while adding cost. Prevention two: fencing tokens. Elections are numbered with a term/epoch; every write carries the leader's term and storage rejects stale terms — so an old leader that froze in a GC pause and never saw the election gets its writes refused when it wakes, instead of corrupting data. In practice you delegate all of this to Raft-based systems or a coordination service (etcd, ZooKeeper) rather than building it. In an interview I bring this up myself whenever I draw automatic failover, because 'how do you know the old leader is really dead?' is the trap the question is built around.
followUps: Why is 'the old leader will notice it lost connectivity and step down' not a sufficient answer?
You have exactly two datacenters and cannot form a majority in either — what are your options?

interviewQA.q: Kafka versus RabbitMQ — how do you choose?
interviewQA.a: I choose by the shape of the work, and I describe the two mental models to show why. Kafka is a distributed append-only log: producers append to partitioned topics, messages are retained for days regardless of consumption, and each consumer group tracks its own offset — so many independent consumers read the same stream at their own pace, replay is a matter of rewinding an offset, ordering holds per partition, and throughput is enormous because appending to a log is nearly free. RabbitMQ is a smart broker for jobs: exchanges route messages into queues, a worker acks a message and it is deleted — rich routing, priorities, per-message acknowledgement, natural fit for 'this task must be done once by one worker'. So: event streams with multiple readers (orders consumed by analytics, search indexing, and fraud detection), replayability after a bug, or six-figure messages per second — Kafka. Task distribution — send email, resize image, run report — with routing rules and simpler operations — RabbitMQ, or a cloud queue like SQS, which I mention because 'boring managed service' is often the honest answer at the scale under discussion. The trap answer is 'Kafka because it is bigger'; retention-plus-offsets versus route-and-delete is the real distinction.
followUps: How does a Kafka consumer group distribute partitions among its members, and what limits parallelism?
You need strict global ordering of all events — what does that cost you in Kafka?

interviewQA.q: Is exactly-once delivery possible? What do you do about duplicates?
interviewQA.a: Exactly-once delivery between independent systems is not achievable in general: the consumer can process a message and crash before its acknowledgement is recorded, and the broker cannot distinguish 'processed, ack lost' from 'never processed' — redelivering risks a duplicate, not redelivering risks a loss. So real systems pick at-least-once (redeliver on missing ack) and engineer duplicates into harmlessness; the honest phrase is effectively-once processing. Recipe one: idempotent consumers — dedupe on a unique message or operation ID; the consumer records the ID with the result in the same transaction as the side effect, and a redelivered ID is answered from the record without re-executing. Recipe two: the transactional outbox for the producing side — write the business row and the outgoing event in one database transaction, and a relay publishes from the outbox table, so 'DB updated but event never sent' cannot happen. On Kafka specifically, idempotent producers and transactions give real exactly-once semantics, but scoped to Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines; the moment the consumer touches an external system — a payment API, an email provider — you are back to idempotency keys. In an interview, saying 'I assume at-least-once and make consumers idempotent' in one sentence signals production experience faster than anything else in this topic.
followUps: Where do you store the dedupe record so that checking it and applying the side effect are atomic?
What is the difference between at-most-once and at-least-once, and when would you ever accept at-most-once?

interviewQA.q: Explain CAP to a junior engineer, then explain what PACELC adds.
interviewQA.a: CAP, stated carefully: when a network partition occurs — nodes are running but cannot reach each other — a distributed system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write, or you return an error) and availability (every request gets an answer, possibly stale). The corrections to the folklore version matter: it is not 'pick two of three', because partitions are not optional — hardware fails, so P is a given and the choice is C-versus-A during partitions only; on a healthy network you can have both. A CP system's minority side refuses writes during a partition (right for payments, inventory, and lock services like ZooKeeper — a lock service that lies is worse than one that is down). An AP system keeps answering on both sides and reconciles later (right for like counts, carts, product views — Dynamo's cart is the canonical example). PACELC adds the 99.9% of life CAP ignores: Else — with no partition — you still trade Latency against Consistency, because strong consistency means coordination (sync replication, quorum reads) and coordination means round trips. Dynamo-style stores are PA/EL: available under partition, fast normally, eventually consistent. HBase-style are PC/EC. The senior move is per-feature classification: in one app, checkout is CP/EC while the feed is AP/EL.
followUps: Why can a single-node database be called CA, and why does that stop making sense once you distribute?
Give a concrete example of the EL/EC choice showing up as a latency number a user would feel.

interviewQA.q: What is read-your-writes consistency, and how do you implement it?
interviewQA.a: It is the session guarantee that a user always sees their own writes, even when everyone else's reads may be stale. The motivating bug: a user changes their avatar, the write lands on the leader, their next page load reads a replica that is two seconds behind, and the old avatar comes back — the user concludes the upload failed, retries, and files a bug. Nothing here needs global strong consistency; only the author needs freshness about their own data. Three implementations, in the order I would offer them. One: after a user writes, pin that user's reads to the leader for a window longer than typical replication lag — say five seconds keyed by user ID; costs a little leader load, easy to build. Two: sticky sessions — route the user to the same replica consistently, which has typically seen their own writes; fragile across replica failover. Three: causal/version tokens — the write returns a log position (an LSN); the client presents it on reads and a replica may answer only after replaying past that position; precise, and it composes across devices if the token is stored server-side per session. I would also name the sibling guarantee, monotonic reads — the user never sees data go backwards when bouncing between replicas with different lag — fixed by the same sticky routing. The interviewer is testing whether I can name a middle ground between 'strong everywhere' (slow) and 'eventual everywhere' (buggy UX).
followUps: The user writes on their phone and immediately reads on their laptop — which of your three implementations still works?
How would you measure replication lag in production, and what alert would you set on it?

interviewQA.q: Design a rate limiter for a public API. Which algorithm and where does it live?
interviewQA.a: Requirements first: per-API-key limits (say 100 requests/sec sustained with brief bursts allowed), enforcement across all gateway instances, cheap enough to run on every request, and friendly rejection — HTTP 429 with Retry-After. Algorithm: token bucket. Each key has a bucket with capacity (max burst, e.g. 200) refilled at a fixed rate (100/sec); a request spends a token, an empty bucket means 429. I pick it over fixed windows because fixed windows leak a double burst at the boundary — 100 requests at 11:59:59 and 100 more at 12:00:01 both pass — and over a sliding log because the bucket needs only two numbers per key (tokens, last-refill time) instead of a timestamp list. Placement: at the API gateway, before requests consume application capacity. State lives in Redis so all gateway instances share one view; the refill-check-decrement must be atomic, so it runs as a small Lua script (or the equivalent single INCR-with-expiry approximation). Failure policy is worth stating: if Redis is unreachable I fail open (allow traffic) for availability, unless the limiter is a security control, in which case fail closed. I would add per-IP limits for unauthenticated endpoints and return rate-limit headers so clients can self-regulate before hitting 429.
followUps: Redis round trips add latency at the gateway — how do you reduce that without losing global accuracy?
How would you rate-limit an abusive client that rotates IP addresses and API keys?

interviewQA.q: What is an idempotency key and in which designs must you volunteer it?
interviewQA.a: An idempotency key is a client-generated unique ID for one logical operation — a UUID minted when the checkout page loads — sent with the request, usually as a header. The server, on first execution, atomically records the key together with the response it produced; when the same key arrives again (client timeout and retry, user double-click, queue redelivery under at-least-once), the server recognises it and replays the stored response without executing the side effect again. The card is charged once no matter how many times the request lands. The atomicity detail is the part interviewers probe: the key must be recorded in the same transaction as the side effect (or via a unique-constraint insert that doubles as a lock), otherwise a crash between 'do the work' and 'record the key' recreates the duplicate problem; keys get a TTL, say 24 hours. Stripe's API popularised the pattern, which makes it a concrete name to cite. You must volunteer it, unprompted, in any design where a retry can repeat a non-idempotent effect: payments, order placement, account creation, any consumer of an at-least-once queue, any POST an external client can retry. Saying 'my queue consumers are idempotent, deduping on the message ID' closes the loop that at-least-once delivery opens — the two concepts are one story, and telling it whole is the senior signal.
followUps: Two requests with the same idempotency key arrive concurrently, not sequentially — what happens in your implementation?
Why is PUT naturally idempotent while POST is not, and how does that shape API design?

interviewQA.q: Why do we alert on p99 latency instead of average latency?
interviewQA.a: Because latency distributions are long-tailed, and the mean is distorted by the tail while describing no real request. Concrete: 100 requests, 99 at 50 ms, one at 5 s — the average is 99.5 ms, which sounds healthy and matches nobody's experience; p50 says the typical user gets 50 ms, p99 says one user in a hundred waits five full seconds. Percentiles are statements about users; averages are statements about arithmetic. The tail matters far more than '1%' suggests, for two reasons. Fan-out: a page that calls 100 backends in parallel is as slow as the slowest call, and the probability that at least one call hits its p99 is 1 - 0.99^100, about 63% — the worst 1% becomes the majority experience of your most complex pages; this is the 'tail at scale' argument. Heavy users: your most valuable users make the most requests, so they sample the tail most often — the tail is where you lose exactly the people you least want to lose. Practically I dashboard p50/p95/p99 per endpoint, alert on SLO burn (e.g. '99.9% of requests under 200 ms over 30 days'), and treat a p99 regression after a deploy as a rollback trigger. Averages I keep only for capacity math, never for user experience.
followUps: Why is it mathematically wrong to average p99 values across ten load-balanced servers, and what do you do instead?
Your p99 is fine but users still complain about slowness — what could the percentiles be hiding?

interviewQA.q: When would you add a CDN, and what belongs on it?
interviewQA.a: I add a CDN the moment the design has media or a geographically spread audience, and I justify it with two numbers. Latency: a cross-continent round trip is ~150 ms before the server does any work, while a nearby edge answers in 10-30 ms — no origin optimisation can beat geography. Bandwidth: if the photo app serves 50K reads/sec at ~2 MB each, that is ~100 GB/s of egress; that traffic must terminate at edge caches, because no sane origin serves it. What belongs on it: anything identical for all users — images, video segments, JS/CSS bundles, fonts, installers — served in pull mode (edge fetches from origin on first miss, caches per Cache-Control TTL); push mode is for pre-positioning known-in-advance content like a video release. The follow-up to pre-empt is invalidation: how do users get app.js v2 while edges hold v1? Version the URLs — a content hash in the filename (app.8f3ab2.js), referenced by the new HTML — so old and new coexist, nothing is purged, and assets can carry year-long TTLs. I also name the limit: a CDN does nothing for personalised responses — the feed and the cart still hit the origin — which is the honest boundary of the tool and the segue to multi-region if the interviewer wants to go there.
followUps: What does a CDN change about your origin's capacity planning — what fraction of traffic still reaches you?
How would you serve private media — say, photos visible only to friends — through a CDN?

interviewQA.q: Your read replica lags 2 seconds behind the leader. What user-visible bugs appear, and what do you do?
interviewQA.a: Three concrete bugs. Read-your-writes violations: a user saves a profile change, the next page load reads the replica, and the edit is gone — they retry or file a bug; fixed by pinning a user's reads to the leader for a few seconds after their own write, or by version tokens (the write returns a log position; a replica may serve the read only after replaying past it). Monotonic-read violations: two refreshes hit replicas with different lag and a comment appears then disappears — time runs backwards; fixed with sticky routing so one session reads one replica. Causality violations: a reply becomes visible before the message it answers, because the two writes replicated in different order to different replicas the readers use. What I do operationally: first measure — export replication lag as a metric per replica and alert on a threshold tied to product tolerance (say 5 s); second, degrade sensibly — the load balancer stops sending reads to a replica whose lag exceeds the bound, trading capacity for correctness; third, be honest about the source — lag spikes usually mean the replica cannot keep up with write volume (undersized replica, long transactions, or a schema migration), so the fix may be on the write path. What I do NOT do is switch everything to synchronous replication reflexively — that converts a freshness bug affecting some reads into a latency tax on every write, which is usually the worse trade.
followUps: The lag alert fires at 30 seconds and keeps climbing — walk me through your diagnosis.
Which reads in an e-commerce app genuinely must go to the leader, and which never should?

flashcards.front: Rough latencies: main-memory reference vs SSD random read vs cross-continent RTT?
flashcards.back: ~100 ns vs ~100 us vs ~150 ms — each step is ~1000x. Datacenter RTT ~500 us; SSD 1 MB sequential ~1 ms; HDD seek ~10 ms. The ratios explain caching (SSD -> memory) and CDNs (far -> near).

flashcards.front: The QPS shortcut: how many seconds in a day, and what is X million requests/day in QPS?
flashcards.back: 86,400 s — round to 10^5. X million requests/day ~ 10·X QPS average (1M/day ~ 12 QPS). Multiply by 2-5x for peak, and say which factor you assumed.

flashcards.front: In estimation, what design decisions does the read:write ratio drive?
flashcards.back: High ratios (100:1, 500:1) justify cache-first design, read replicas, and CDNs; write-heavy workloads point to queues, batching, and LSM-style stores. Say the conclusion out loud: 'read-heavy, so cache-first.'

flashcards.front: L4 vs L7 load balancer — one line each?
flashcards.back: L4 = transport layer: sees IP/port only, forwards packets, extremely fast, content-blind. L7 = application layer: terminates TLS, reads HTTP, routes by path/header/cookie, sticky sessions — costs CPU. Web/API -> L7; raw TCP or non-HTTP throughput -> L4.

flashcards.front: When does 'least connections' beat round robin for load balancing?
flashcards.back: When request durations vary a lot: round robin takes turns and piles long requests onto unlucky servers; least-connections routes each new request to the server with the fewest open connections, tracking actual load.

flashcards.front: Active vs passive health checks on a load balancer?
flashcards.back: Active: LB polls GET /health every few seconds, ejects after ~3 consecutive failures, re-admits on recovery. Passive: LB watches real traffic and ejects backends returning errors/timeouts. Without them the LB keeps routing users into a dead server.

flashcards.front: Cache-aside: the read path in 3 steps, and the write rule?
flashcards.back: Read: check cache -> on miss read DB -> populate cache with TTL. Write: update DB, then DELETE the cache key so the next read repopulates. Only hot data gets cached, and the app survives a cache outage (if the DB can carry full read load).

flashcards.front: Write-through vs write-behind caching — the trade?
flashcards.back: Write-through: write cache + DB synchronously — fresh reads, slower writes. Write-behind: ack after writing cache only, flush to DB async — fast writes, but a cache-node crash loses unflushed writes. Fine for counters, wrong for orders.

flashcards.front: Cache stampede (thundering herd): what happens and the three fixes?
flashcards.back: A hot key expires; thousands of concurrent misses fire the same query and flatten the DB. Fixes: (1) per-key single-flight lock — one rebuilds, others wait/serve stale; (2) stale-while-revalidate; (3) TTL jitter so keys don't expire together.

flashcards.front: Why add random jitter to cache TTLs?
flashcards.back: Keys populated together (deploy, cache flush, batch warm-up) expire together, creating synchronized miss storms. A random offset per key spreads expiries so the DB refills the cache gradually instead of all at once.

flashcards.front: Redis ballpark numbers to quote in an interview?
flashcards.back: In-memory KV store: sub-millisecond reads, ~100K ops/sec per node; scale further by clustering/sharding. Also the standard home for sessions, rate-limit counters, distributed locks, and leaderboards (sorted sets).

flashcards.front: Pull CDN vs push CDN?
flashcards.back: Pull: edge fetches from origin on first miss, caches per Cache-Control TTL — default for websites, no upload workflow. Push: you upload ahead of time — for content with a known release moment (video episodes, game patches).

flashcards.front: How do users get the new version of a CDN-cached file without purging?
flashcards.back: Version the URL: put a content hash in the filename (app.8f3ab2.js) and reference the new name from the HTML. Old and new coexist, nothing is purged, and assets can carry year-long TTLs. Purge APIs are the slow, forgettable fallback.

flashcards.front: What is a read replica and what is its inherent cost?
flashcards.back: A DB copy receiving the leader's writes and serving reads — multiplies read capacity cheaply. Cost: replication lag, so reads can be stale; a user may write then read the old value (read-your-writes violation) unless you pin or version their reads.

flashcards.front: Range sharding vs hash sharding — the one trade each?
flashcards.back: Range: contiguous key ranges per shard — range scans stay on one shard, but hot ranges ('this month') overload one node. Hash: even spread, but range queries must fan out to every shard. Directory-based adds flexibility at the cost of an extra hop.

flashcards.front: What fraction of keys move when hash(key) % N goes from 3 to 4 nodes?
flashcards.back: About 75% (in general ~N/(N+1) move) — nearly every key changes owner, forcing mass migration and cold caches. This is the resharding pain that consistent hashing exists to fix.

flashcards.front: Consistent hashing: what moves when you add a node, and what are virtual nodes for?
flashcards.back: Nodes and keys hash onto a ring; a key belongs to the first node clockwise. Adding a node moves only its arc — ~1/N of keys — so caches stay warm. Virtual nodes (each server at 100+ ring points) even out arc sizes and spread a departing node's load across many peers.

flashcards.front: Two properties a good shard key must have?
flashcards.back: (1) Spreads load evenly — no hot partition (beware celebrity users, 'today' timestamps); (2) appears in the dominant queries — a query without the shard key fans out to every shard, and cross-shard joins/transactions become application code.

flashcards.front: Sync vs async replication — the trade in one line, and the middle path?
flashcards.back: Sync: ack after a follower confirms — zero loss on failover, every write pays an RTT and stalls on slow followers. Async: ack immediately — fast, but failover can lose the last seconds of acknowledged writes. Semi-sync: wait for one follower (or quorum), bounding loss.

flashcards.front: Quorum: the formula, and why clusters have odd sizes?
flashcards.back: Majority = floor(N/2)+1. Five nodes need 3, tolerating 2 failures; six nodes still tolerate only 2 — even sizes add cost without fault tolerance. Two disjoint majorities cannot exist, which is what makes quorum prevent split brain.

flashcards.front: What is split brain and the two structural defenses?
flashcards.back: A partition leaves two groups each electing a leader; both accept writes and data diverges irreconcilably. Defenses: quorum (only a majority side can elect) and fencing tokens (numbered terms; storage rejects writes stamped with an old term, stopping a paused-and-revived old leader).

flashcards.front: Three reasons to put a message queue between two services?
flashcards.back: (1) Decouple availability — producer succeeds while consumer is down; (2) absorb spikes — queue buffers 50K/min in while workers drain 10K/min; (3) decouple latency — respond to the user now, do slow work (email, thumbnails, fan-out) async.

flashcards.front: At-least-once delivery: what does it force on every consumer?
flashcards.back: Idempotency. The broker redelivers anything unacked (e.g. consumer crashed after the work, before the ack), so duplicates are guaranteed eventually. Consumers dedupe on a message/operation ID recorded atomically with the side effect.

flashcards.front: The 'effectively-once' recipe, since exactly-once delivery is impossible across systems?
flashcards.back: At-least-once delivery PLUS idempotent processing: dedupe table keyed by message ID written in the same transaction as the side effect; add a transactional outbox on the producer so the DB write and the event publish cannot diverge.

flashcards.front: Kafka in one mental model?
flashcards.back: A distributed, partitioned, append-only log. Messages are retained (days) regardless of consumption; consumer groups track offsets, so many independent readers replay at will; ordering holds per partition; throughput is huge because appends are cheap.

flashcards.front: When RabbitMQ (or SQS) over Kafka?
flashcards.back: When the unit is a job done once by one worker — send email, resize image — with routing rules, priorities, per-message acks, and simpler ops. Kafka wins for event streams with multiple independent consumers, replay, and very high throughput.

flashcards.front: State CAP correctly, avoiding the 'pick two of three' folklore.
flashcards.back: During a network partition, choose consistency (refuse/error rather than serve stale) or availability (answer, possibly stale). Partitions are not optional, so the choice is C-vs-A under partition only; a healthy network gives both. CP: payments, ZooKeeper. AP: likes, carts, Cassandra.

flashcards.front: What does PACELC add to CAP?
flashcards.back: The no-partition case: Else, trade Latency vs Consistency — strong consistency needs coordination (sync replication, quorum reads), which costs round trips on every operation. Dynamo-style = PA/EL; HBase-style = PC/EC. Classify per feature, not per company.

flashcards.front: Linearizability (strong consistency) in one sentence?
flashcards.back: The system behaves as if there were a single copy: once a write is acknowledged, every subsequent read anywhere returns it (or newer). Free on one node; on replicas it is paid for with quorum/sync coordination, i.e. latency.

flashcards.front: Read-your-writes consistency: the guarantee and three implementations?
flashcards.back: A user always sees their OWN writes (others may lag). Implement by: (1) pinning the writer's reads to the leader for ~lag window; (2) sticky sessions to one replica; (3) version tokens — write returns a log position, replicas serve the read only after replaying past it.

flashcards.front: Token bucket: the two parameters and what each controls?
flashcards.back: capacity = max burst allowed at once; refill rate = sustained requests/sec. Each request spends a token; empty bucket -> HTTP 429 + Retry-After. State is two numbers per key in Redis, updated atomically (Lua).

flashcards.front: What is wrong with fixed-window rate limiting?
flashcards.back: The boundary burst: with '100/minute', 100 requests at 11:59:59 plus 100 at 12:00:01 all pass — double the intended rate in two seconds. Sliding windows or token buckets close the hole.

flashcards.front: Idempotency key: the flow in three steps?
flashcards.back: Client mints a unique key per logical operation (UUID at checkout load) and sends it as a header. Server records key + response atomically with the side effect on first execution. A retry with the same key replays the stored response — the card is charged once.

flashcards.front: p99 latency: definition, and why the average lies?
flashcards.back: 99% of requests are faster than the p99 value; 1% are slower. Averages hide the skewed tail: 99 requests at 50 ms + one at 5 s averages ~100 ms — a number matching no real request. Percentiles describe users; means describe arithmetic.

flashcards.front: Fan out to 100 backends: what is the chance a request hits at least one backend's p99?
flashcards.back: 1 - 0.99^100 ~ 63%. The worst 1% becomes the majority experience of complex pages — the 'tail at scale' argument, and the reason p99 (not average) is what you engineer and alert on.

flashcards.front: The four golden signals to monitor on every service?
flashcards.back: Latency (p50/p95/p99, never the mean), traffic (QPS), errors (5xx rate), saturation (fullness of the constraining resource: CPU, connections, queue depth). Alert on symptoms users feel — SLO burn — not on raw causes like 'CPU 80%'.

flashcards.front: SLI vs SLO vs error budget?
flashcards.back: SLI = the measured indicator ('fraction of requests under 200 ms'). SLO = the target ('99.9% over 30 days'). Error budget = 100% minus SLO — allowed failure; when it is spent, reliability work pre-empts feature work.
